query: Fix slow mobile product-page hero images without delaying the LCP image

cards.title: Lazy-load below-the-fold images but never the hero image
cards.summary: Apply lazy loading to off-screen images to cut initial download, while forcing the main hero/in-view image to load eagerly to protect LCP.
cards.use_when: Setting theme image behavior or debugging slow perceived load / poor LCP on homepage banners and product grids.
steps: Leave the main hero image (the banner at the top) loading eagerly — do not lazy-load it, because in-view images are usually the Largest Contentful Paint element and lazy-loading them worsens LCP, which the source says Google dislikes.
Apply lazy loading (loading="lazy") to everything below the fold: lower section images, secondary product images, and decorative overlays.
If your theme's hero section lazy-loads its first image by default, add custom logic to exempt that first image so it renders immediately.
Verify behavior in the browser/network panel: the in-view images should download right away, with further images downloading only as the user scrolls.
caveats: The presenter cautions that if you already have serious LCP or CLS problems, lazy-loading fixes won't be enough — those issues need separate attention.
Theme behavior differs by theme version; verify the current interface and default markup.

cards.title: Fix LCP by Un-lazy-loading and De-animating the Hero Image
cards.summary: The largest contentful paint is usually the hero; it must load eagerly with no lazy attribute, no fade-in and maximum compression.
cards.use_when: Improving a poor LCP reading on a homepage, category page or any page where a large hero dominates.
steps: Identify the largest element — typically the hero banner image or the first slide of a slider.
Remove loading="lazy" and any lazy-sizes classes or loading-lazy patterns from that image; the source says this should never be lazy loaded.
Set loading="eager" instead, telling the browser the image is important and should load as fast as possible.
Remove fade-in, slide-in or other entrance effects from that image, since effects force an effects library download before the image shows.
Compress the image as much as you can once the loading behaviour is correct.
In a slider, implement logic so the first image is never lazy loaded or animated while later slides can be; also check blocking time, which affects LCP too.
caveats: In his example the image was lazy loaded and should have said eager — but LCP can also be driven by blocking time and effects, so check more than the loading attribute.

cards.title: Optimize LCP: Compress, Serve via CDN, Unblock Rendering
cards.summary: Four mechanical levers for pulling Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds on storefront pages.
cards.use_when: After you've identified your LCP element and need concrete fixes for your hero image, category tiles, or above-the-fold content.
steps: Reduce resource load time: compress images and move to modern formats like WebP; reduce fonts to the bare minimum needed to render the page, since each font is a downloaded asset.
Serve assets from a CDN. The source notes deploying to platforms like Firebase or Vercel handles CDN delivery automatically, so you don't manually manage edge caching.

Eliminate render-blocking JavaScript above the fold. If scripts must execute before the hero image displays, they delay LCP. The source cites this as a reason server-side frameworks (e.g., Next.js) beat client-only single-page apps like plain React on initial load—SPAs must run a lot of JS before main content renders.
Use preload links so important assets are discovered first by the browser, and set fetchpriority to high on critical above-the-fold images so low-priority below-fold images don't compete with them.
caveats: Switching rendering architecture (SPA to SSR) is a major rebuild, not a quick tactical fix; only pursue it if the simpler levers are insufficient.
The source's deployment-platform CDN behavior is a snapshot and vendor interfaces change—verify current behavior in your platform's docs.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: LCP diagnosis: the largest-in-viewport element and its delay source
cards.summary: Identify what the largest contentful paint element actually is, then remove whatever mechanism delays its display rather than optimizing unrelated assets.
cards.use_when: Product or landing page speed audit where Google PageSpeed shows a poor LCP score and you need to decide what to fix first.
steps: Run the PageSpeed/Google test on the actual PDP or landing page you send paid traffic to, not the homepage. The source notes that even when the homepage scores fine, the page receiving ad traffic often has a huge LCP problem.

Open Chrome DevTools, go to the Network tab, disable cache and set throttling to fast or slow 3G, then reload. Watch what actually renders. In the reviewed store the layout and secondary images appeared, but the main product image did not — the image file was already downloaded but not shown.

Trace why it isn't shown. In the reviewed example the cause was a slideshow/carousel plugin: its JavaScript had to load before the first big image rendered, so the image sat hidden even after downloading.

Fix the delay at its source: keep the main product image out of the lazy-loaded carousel path, use a plain img that renders immediately, and remove any preloader/placeholder that hides the in-view image.

Add a preload link for that specific image in the head (see the preload card) and consider a more benefit-legible main image, since a confusing main image also hurts comprehension when the shopper lands from an ad.
Re-test three times and average the results to confirm the change is constant rather than a one-off test.
caveats: The source's affected store measured around 5 seconds LCP before and expected roughly 50-60 after a preload fix; treat these as that store's numbers, not benchmarks.
Desktop often already scores acceptably; the source focuses mobile because that is where slow-connection shoppers experience the store.
Editing theme.liquid requires a theme backup or duplicate before publishing.

cards.title: Fix LCP by identifying the largest element and optimizing it
cards.summary: LCP measures how long the largest above-the-fold element takes to load; identify that element in lab diagnostics, then optimize it by type.
cards.use_when: Improving page speed on a product page or homepage where the hero image, banner, or headline is the first thing shoppers see.
steps: Treat LCP under 2.5s as good (green), 2.5–4.0s as needs improvement (orange), and over 4.0s as poor (red) — these are the thresholds the source states.
Find the LCP element: in lab data, expand Diagnostics and open 'Largest Contentful Paint element' to see exactly what it is (image, video, or text block).
If it is an image: resize to the dimensions actually rendered, compress the file below roughly 250KB, and serve in a modern format such as WebP or AVIF.
If it is a video: compress the file to reduce its size.
If it is text: leave it. The source's opinion is that a text LCP is the fastest-loading option, so prefer a text-led hero when design allows.
Remember that a slow LCP is usually not a web server problem — the source attributes it mainly to your theme, plugins, and the page elements you placed.
caveats: The 250KB image guidance and text-LCP preference are the source's recommendations, not vendor-published requirements.
The 1,200px recommended image width mentioned in the source is tied to Google Discover eligibility, not LCP itself.
cards.source_name: Google PageSpeed Insights_ Step-by-Step tutorial to Boost Site Speed.docx

query: Audit Shopify app scripts while preserving add-to-cart and purchase tracking

cards.title: Reduce storefront script blocking while preserving purchase tracking
cards.summary: Audit script loading without breaking product interactions or analytics events.
cards.use_when: Reducing JavaScript render blocking in a Shopify theme's liquid files
steps: Inventory theme and app scripts; remove confirmed unused integrations on a duplicate theme first.
Choose defer or async only after checking execution order, DOM dependencies and the vendor integration requirements.
Do not impose a blanket synchronous-pixel rule. Use the supported platform integration; Shopify provides a Web Pixels API and standard event subscriptions.
Test consent behavior, page views, variant selection, add-to-cart and a test purchase after changes; check missing and duplicate events.
caveats: Editorial correction: source advice that all pixels must remain synchronous is not a universal requirement. Verify the specific integration. https://shopify.dev/docs/api/pixels

cards.title: Audit theme.liquid for Scripts Missing defer or async
cards.summary: Loop through theme.liquid scripts and add defer (or async) to third-party tags that block rendering.
cards.use_when: Starting a Shopify speed audit or after the major app-script issues are addressed.
steps: Open theme.liquid and scan for script tags lacking a defer or async attribute; Shopify now flags these for you.
For each, identify which app it belongs to (e.g. the source traced a script to an 'ILO Banner' cookie banner) and choose which attribute to apply.
Prefer defer: async loads alongside the page, while defer waits until the site is downloaded and then fetches the script, producing less blocking time.
Add it as either defer or defer="defer" — both work identically.
Test whether the app still functions after adding defer; in the source's case the cookie banner still worked, meaning it didn't truly need to load immediately.
caveats: Some apps break if their scripts are deferred and genuinely require immediate execution.
Expect small gains from this alone — it's a cleanup step, not a headline fix.

cards.title: Audit Shopify theme files for leftover app code with a code editor
cards.summary: Open the theme export in a code editor and search for app names to find and remove residual pixel and tracking code slowing the store.
cards.use_when: Store speed work is blocked or polluted by old app scripts you can no longer control from the Shopify admin, and you need to locate the exact theme file and line before deleting anything.
steps: Download your theme (Online Store > Themes > ... > Download theme file) and unzip it, or open it directly in a code editor such as Cursor (free; has AI assistance if you don't write code) using Open Folder.
Use the editor's global search to find app keywords, e.g. 'hexom' for an uninstalled app, 'Google' for Google-related tags, or 'logs' for a reviews app. See which files contain them.
When you open a match, note the file name and the approximate line number (e.g. a pixel at line 72 of a .json or .liquid file).
Back in Shopify, go to Theme > Edit code, search the same file, jump to the nearby line, and remove only the target tag/code.
Save and verify the store still works before doing the next removal; only remove code you have positively matched to an app you no longer use.
caveats: Editing live theme code can break functionality or checkout; test after each change and keep a downloaded backup of the original theme.
The source stresses confirming what a script does before altering it, because some apps require their scripts to load immediately.

cards.title: Cut Third-Party App and Script Bloat Without Losing Functionality
cards.summary: How to audit installed apps/plugins, understand their performance cost, and decide which to remove, defer or async-load — the source calls script count the strongest predictor of mobile speed.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing your installed apps and plugins, or deciding whether to install a new one, and need a repeatable audit that protects mobile performance.
steps: Quantify the problem: in the source's Shopify Speed Benchmark (1,533 stores), correlation between third-party service count and performance score was r = -0.66, the dataset's strongest signal. Stores with 0-5 services scored a median 74 on mobile; stores with 21-30 dropped to 44.
Audit regularly: list every app, plugin, chat widget, review tool, upsell popup and analytics tag, then remove tools you no longer actively use. Each adds JavaScript running on every page load.
Before installing anything new: check reviews for speed complaints. After installing: run a speed test to measure impact. Remove apps that degrade performance without delivering proportional value.
For scripts you must keep, defer or async-load those that don't affect initial rendering so they download after main content — this improves INP by reducing JS execution during page load.

Account for industry stack weight when setting expectations: source cites beauty stores loading a median 31 third-party services per page (worst of 9 Shopify industries for mobile speed) and automotive parts stores a median of 15 (best), with fashion/apparel in between due to sizing charts and shipping insurance.
Guard against gradual degradation: performance declines silently as products, apps and tracking scripts accumulate, so schedule the audit rather than waiting for complaints or a conversion drop.
caveats: The median-score and correlation figures come from the source's own benchmark dataset of Shopify stores; treat them as directional, not as targets your store must match.
Removing apps can drop functionality customers expect — weight each removal against its feature value, not just its byte cost.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Site Speed Optimization_ Complete Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Audit and remove third-party apps slowing your Shopify store
cards.summary: Shows how app scripts enter the theme head via content_for_header and how to decide whether an app's value justifies its speed cost.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a bloated app stack or evaluating whether to install one more app on a Shopify store.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: most script and CSS files for apps installed through Shopify Admin are injected into the <head> of theme.liquid through the {{ content_for_header }} object, and an app must be rendered before other code loads.
Note the source's threshold: if you have more than 20 plugins installed, you likely aren't using them all, yet they still run in the background and can hurt performance.
Enlist a developer to remove unnecessary apps, including forgotten trials.
Re-test after removals using PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix, or Chrome DevTools' Network tab (reload the page with the tab open) to see the effect.
Before any new install, ask whether the app's added value outweighs the possible load-speed penalty.

Understand the async nuance from Shopify's Jason Bowman: scripts added via the Script Tag API are async-loaded so page load isn't halted, but scripts added directly into the <head> often impact performance immediately. Prefer the API path where available.
caveats: The 20-plugin figure is a heuristic, not a cutoff; an app's weight matters more than its count.
Third-party app code isn't fully under your control, so removing apps may need developer support.
Shopify's app-injection and Script Tag behaviors may change; verify against current documentation.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

query: Configure WooCommerce caching without caching customer carts or checkout

cards.title: Caching Layers: What to Cache, What Never to Cache
cards.summary: Browser, CDN edge and server-side caching for ecommerce, plus the hard rule that cart, checkout and account pages must never be cached.
cards.use_when: You are configuring cache headers or a CDN and need to set safe durations and exclusion rules for user-specific ecommerce pages.
steps: Browser caching: instruct visitor browsers to store static assets (CSS, JS, images) locally. Set long expiration dates — the source suggests up to a year for static assets since filenames change when content updates. HTML pages need shorter durations so visitors see current content.

CDN edge caching: store content on globally distributed servers so a visitor in Tokyo is served from an Asian edge instead of a US origin. The source cites 200-800ms latency reduction for geographically distant visitors.

Server-side caching: store generated HTML or database query results so the server doesn't rebuild pages per visitor. WooCommerce options include WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache and Redis Object Cache; Shopify manages this automatically with limited control.
Never cache cart pages, checkout flows or account pages — they contain visitor-specific data and caching them causes serious errors.

Handle session cookies carefully: the source cites Salesforce guidance to defer session creation until the visitor actually needs it (first add-to-cart or login), which keeps anonymous browsing cacheable.
Handle volatile data like prices and stock status: either cache the page and update those elements dynamically via JavaScript, or use short cache durations with rapid invalidation when data changes.
Audit cache headers after changes to confirm updated content appears correctly while static assets stay cached — misconfiguration causes either stale prices or missed optimization.
caveats: Shopify gives limited control over server-side caching, so some layers may not apply on that platform.
Aggressive asset caching requires a cache-busting filename strategy (e.g., hashed filenames) or visitors will see stale CSS/JS.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Site Speed Optimization_ Complete Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Platform-native caching and intelligent cache invalidation
cards.summary: Using built-in full-page cache, automatic WebP, thumbnail sets and selective invalidation instead of manual workarounds.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring an ecommerce platform's performance features, especially where price and stock updates must not serve stale pages.
steps: Use the platform's integrated HTTP cache so repeat visits are served pre-rendered HTML rather than re-executing PHP and querying the database.
Rely on native WebP generation for uploaded images and automatic thumbnail sets so each device receives an appropriately sized file without a custom pipeline.

Understand intelligent cache invalidation: the platform detects price or stock changes and clears only the affected pages rather than purging the entire site cache — keeping the store fast without displaying outdated prices or availability.
Confirm your platform also bundles and optimises required CSS and JavaScript, avoiding site-wide loading of code needed on only one subpage.
Where your platform lacks these features, look for equivalent automatic image conversion, responsive thumbnail generation and selective cache purging before building custom tooling.
caveats: Shopware 6 is the source's example of a platform with these native features; other platforms differ, so verify current capabilities in your own admin and documentation.
Selective invalidation depends on correct price/stock event wiring — test that price and availability changes actually propagate before trusting the cache.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Common Speed Mistakes and How to Prevent Them
cards.summary: A prevention checklist of the recurring ecommerce speed errors — unoptimized uploads, unaudited apps, ignored mobile, misconfigured caching, neglected fonts and databases.
cards.use_when: You are auditing store speed hygiene or building a process to stop new speed regressions from being introduced.
steps: Never upload unoptimized images: resize to actual display dimensions and compress before upload. A 4000x3000 photo at full quality can exceed 5MB, longer than some customers will wait.

Never install an app without a speed check: check reviews for speed complaints before installing, and test page speed after to measure impact. Remove apps that degrade performance without proportional value.

Never assume desktop tests reflect mobile: mobile devices have less processing power and often slower connections. Test mobile specifically and prioritize mobile optimizations — the majority of ecommerce visits are mobile.
Avoid caching misconfiguration: too-aggressive caching serves stale prices or stock status; too-conservative caching forfeits the benefit. Audit cache headers after changes.
Optimize fonts: host fonts locally or use font-display: swap to show fallback text while custom fonts load, and subset fonts to include only the characters you use.

Clean the database on database-driven platforms: old revisions, expired transients and orphaned metadata bloat WooCommerce and similar platforms. Schedule regular cleanup with plugins like WP-Optimize.
Test more than once: performance varies by server load, network and cache state, so a single test is a snapshot, not a trend.
caveats: This is a prevention checklist, not a diagnostic ranking — the priority ladder (images, scripts, hosting) still governs fix order.
Database cleanup tools differ by platform; Shopify stores have far less database access than WooCommerce, so this step applies mainly to self-hosted platforms.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Site Speed Optimization_ Complete Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Layer Caching in Browser and on Server Without Over-Relying On It
cards.summary: Temporarily store product data and content so it can be served faster, while keeping the response strategy lean enough that caching is not doing the heavy lifting.
cards.use_when: Repeatedly serving the same product data across category listings and product pages where re-fetching is adding latency.
steps: Cache product data and other content so it is available more quickly, both in the user's browser and on the server.
Treat caching as one layer, not the answer: the source notes that fast, well-structured APIs reduce the amount of caching needed to deliver the same content.
Measure before and after caching changes to confirm the shopper-visible paint actually moved.
Review cache lifetimes against how often product data — stock, price, promotions — actually changes.
caveats: Caching stale product data risks showing wrong prices or availability; set lifetimes against your actual data volatility.
cards.source_name: Page Speed Optimization_ How to Improve the Loading Time of Your Online Shop.docx

cards.title: Don't Trust Third-Party Caching Scripts on Shopify
cards.summary: Shopify already caches store files, so a caching service script adds little and can be left alone.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a speed tool or script that claims to speed up a Shopify store via caching.
steps: Identify scripts on your store belonging to unknown speed or caching services.
Test the actual impact by commenting the script out and re-running speed tests; the source found speed remained essentially the same.
Given Shopify handles caching automatically, don't add a caching service expecting gains, and don't remove a script you don't understand unless testing proves it's inert.
If a mystery script's effect is unknown, leave it alone rather than risk breaking storefront behavior.
caveats: Based on the source's informal testing of one such script, not a controlled study.

context:
[9490c0550ad41c01bd37791a] Caching Layers: What to Cache, What Never to Cache
Use when: You are configuring cache headers or a CDN and need to set safe durations and exclusion rules for user-specific ecommerce pages.
- Browser caching: instruct visitor browsers to store static assets (CSS, JS, images) locally. Set long expiration dates — the source suggests up to a year for static assets since filenames change when content updates. HTML pages need shorter durations so visitors see current content.
- CDN edge caching: store content on globally distributed servers so a visitor in Tokyo is served from an Asian edge instead of a US origin. The source cites 200-800ms latency reduction for geographically distant visitors.
- Server-side caching: store generated HTML or database query results so the server doesn't rebuild pages per visitor. WooCommerce options include WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache and Redis Object Cache; Shopify manages this automatically with limited control.
- Never cache cart pages, checkout flows or account pages — they contain visitor-specific data and caching them causes serious errors.
- Handle session cookies carefully: the source cites Salesforce guidance to defer session creation until the visitor actually needs it (first add-to-cart or login), which keeps anonymous browsing cacheable.
- Handle volatile data like prices and stock status: either cache the page and update those elements dynamically via JavaScript, or use short cache durations with rapid invalidation when data changes.
- Audit cache headers after changes to confirm updated content appears correctly while static assets stay cached — misconfiguration causes either stale prices or missed optimization.
Caveat: Shopify gives limited control over server-side caching, so some layers may not apply on that platform.
Caveat: Aggressive asset caching requires a cache-busting filename strategy (e.g., hashed filenames) or visitors will see stale CSS/JS.

[ee4655c50df6811c3129998d] Platform-native caching and intelligent cache invalidation
Use when: Choosing or configuring an ecommerce platform's performance features, especially where price and stock updates must not serve stale pages.
- Use the platform's integrated HTTP cache so repeat visits are served pre-rendered HTML rather than re-executing PHP and querying the database.
- Rely on native WebP generation for uploaded images and automatic thumbnail sets so each device receives an appropriately sized file without a custom pipeline.
- Understand intelligent cache invalidation: the platform detects price or stock changes and clears only the affected pages rather than purging the entire site cache — keeping the store fast without displaying outdated prices or availability.
- Confirm your platform also bundles and optimises required CSS and JavaScript, avoiding site-wide loading of code needed on only one subpage.
- Where your platform lacks these features, look for equivalent automatic image conversion, responsive thumbnail generation and selective cache purging before building custom tooling.
Caveat: Shopware 6 is the source's example of a platform with these native features; other platforms differ, so verify current capabilities in your own admin and documentation.
Caveat: Selective invalidation depends on correct price/stock event wiring — test that price and availability changes actually propagate before trusting the cache.

[74fc1378fc6aca7a8e1a5745] Common Speed Mistakes and How to Prevent Them
Use when: You are auditing store speed hygiene or building a process to stop new speed regressions from being introduced.
- Never upload unoptimized images: resize to actual display dimensions and compress before upload. A 4000x3000 photo at full quality can exceed 5MB, longer than some customers will wait.
- Never install an app without a speed check: check reviews for speed complaints before installing, and test page speed after to measure impact. Remove apps that degrade performance without proportional value.
- Never assume desktop tests reflect mobile: mobile devices have less processing power and often slower connections. Test mobile specifically and prioritize mobile optimizations — the majority of ecommerce visits are mobile.
- Avoid caching misconfiguration: too-aggressive caching serves stale prices or stock status; too-conservative caching forfeits the benefit. Audit cache headers after changes.
- Optimize fonts: host fonts locally or use font-display: swap to show fallback text while custom fonts load, and subset fonts to include only the characters you use.
- Clean the database on database-driven platforms: old revisions, expired transients and orphaned metadata bloat WooCommerce and similar platforms. Schedule regular cleanup with plugins like WP-Optimize.
- Test more than once: performance varies by server load, network and cache state, so a single test is a snapshot, not a trend.
Caveat: This is a prevention checklist, not a diagnostic ranking — the priority ladder (images, scripts, hosting) still governs fix order.
Caveat: Database cleanup tools differ by platform; Shopify stores have far less database access than WooCommerce, so this step applies mainly to self-hosted platforms.
